name: Treaty with the Ute, 1868 (Kit Carson Treaty)
nations: Núuchi-u (Ute): Tabeguache (Uncompahgre), Muache, Capote, Weeminuche, Yampa, Grand River and Uintah bands; today the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe and Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
promises: Article 2 set apart roughly the western third of Colorado Territory for the 'absolute and undisturbed use and occupation' of the bands, and the United States 'solemnly' agreed that no unauthorized persons would ever pass over, settle upon or reside in it.
Article 16: no cession of any part of the reservation held in common would be valid unless signed by at least three-fourths of the adult men occupying or interested in it.
Articles 11 and 12: up to $30,000 a year for thirty years for clothing and blankets, and up to $30,000 a year for food, as Congress judged necessary.
Articles 9 and 15: seeds and tools for families who farmed, and teachers, carpenters, millers, farmers and blacksmiths.

breaches.what: Miners entered the San Juan region of the reservation, and by the time the Brunot Agreement was signed on September 13, 1873 there were 1,441 mining claims recorded in the area. On the Utes' claim that the consideration was unconscionable, the Indian Claims Commission found the ceded area (Royce Area 566) worth $8,500,000 on April 29, 1874, credited the $507,662.84 paid, and awarded the net $7,992,337.16, subject to offsets.

breaches.what: After the 1879 killings at the White River agency, Congress passed the Act of June 15, 1880. The Supreme Court described it as Congress taking steps to punish the Indians, to dispossess the Utes of their reservation and to remove them from Colorado. The White River and Uncompahgre Utes departed for Utah before 1882, leaving only the Southern Utes in Colorado (402 U.S. 159).

breaches.quote: to dispossess the Utes of their reservation, and to remove them from Colorado

breaches.what: The Southern Ute Indian Tribe states that the Brunot Agreement took reservation land secured in 1868 by fraud, because the Utes were led to believe they were permitting mining only in the San Juan Mountains while keeping about four million acres, and were then forced to relinquish that land as well.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Southern Ute Indian Tribe, tribal history page

landTaken: The Supreme Court (1971) describes the 1868 reservation as approximately 15.7 million acres wholly within Colorado, reduced by the Brunot Cession of 3.7 million acres (Royce Area 566) and then by the 1880 Act, after which only the Southern Utes remained in Colorado.
compensation: $7,908,586.16 final judgment for the Brunot cession (ICC Docket 327, 1965). Court of Claims consent judgments in 1950 for lands ceded under the 1880 Act exceeded $31 million in aggregate (United States v. Southern Ute Tribe, 1971). See also cession-1880-03-06-uta.
today: The Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute reservations in southwestern Colorado and the Uintah and Ouray Reservation in Utah are what remains of the bands' lands.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history says the 1868 reservation covered the western half of Colorado, about 56 million acres, and that Utes remember the 1873 Brunot Agreement as the fraudulent taking of that land: they believed they were allowing mining only in the San Juan Mountains but were forced to give up far more.

openQuestions: Whether the Brunot Agreement was signed by three-fourths of the adult men as Article 16 required was not checked.

The 1880 agreement was put to the Ute bands for consent; whether three-fourths signed, and the Ute account of how signatures were gathered, were not researched. It is recorded here as an Act of Congress because the Supreme Court describes its purpose as dispossession and removal, not as a finding that consent was lacking.

The Southern Ute Indian Tribe's history page is recorded (nation-statement and nationVoice); the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe and the Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation accounts were not found in this pass. (Audit 2026-11-08: this question previously said no nation account was recorded, which no longer matched the file.)

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1965 final judgment changed from claims-commission to litigation, because it was entered on a stipulation compromising the offsets (Docket 327, Final Judgment, February 18, 1965). The 1962 breach no longer says "so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable": in the scan those words are the petitioner's contention, and the Commission's own conclusion is not legible beyond the award. "Within two years ... moved to Utah" replaced by the Supreme Court's "departed for Utah before 1882".
